rounds.proof_sketch: The mutation changes `>` to `>=` in the max-finding loop. When row_logits[i] equals max_val, the original skips the assignment while the mutant performs it. However, since the values are EQUAL by the comparison condition, assigning max_val = row_logits[i] leaves max_val unchanged in value. Loop range: i ∈ [1, num_classes-1] = [1, 9]. For any distinct values, both algorithms find the same maximum. For equal values, both produce the same final max_val value (potentially different index, but index is never used).
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation only affects which tied element's value gets assigned to max_val during the maximum-finding loop. Since tied values are by definition equal, the final value of max_val is identical regardless of which assignment path is taken. The downstream computation only uses the VALUE of max_val (in `row_logits[i] - max_val` and `logf(sum_exp) + max_val`), never any index. Even edge cases like -0.0 vs +0.0 (which have different bit patterns but compare equal) produce identical results because: (1) exp(x - (-0)) = exp(x - (+0)) for all x, and (2) log(sum) + (-0) = log(sum) + (+0) for positive sum. Since sum_exp >= 1 always (contains exp(0)=1 for the max element), log_sum_exp is always positive, absorbing any ±0 difference.
rounds.kill_strategy: The mutant is unkillable because the changed comparison only affects assignment when values are equal, and assigning an equal value to max_val produces no observable change in any downstream computation. No value pattern within fixed shapes can expose a behavioral difference.
rounds.recommendations: When mutating comparison operators in max/min-finding loops, static equivalence rules should recognize that `if (x > max) max = x` is semantically equivalent to `if (x >= max) max = x` when only the VALUE (not index) of the maximum is used downstream. This pattern represents a classic semantic equivalence that mutation testing frameworks should detect.
